statement: Fifteen minutes remain. Rosa has five questions left and knows how long each would take: 3 points in 4 min, 4 points in 3 min, 4 points in 5 min, 5 points in 7 min and 5 points in 8 min. What is the most points she can score from questions she fully solves in time?

choices.misconception: I did the two 5-point questions first because they are worth the most, and that used up all 15 minutes.
I always took the question with the most points per minute next, which left 3 minutes unused and only 11 points.
I started with the quicker 5-point question and then filled the time with the quickest of the rest.
I added up the points for all five questions without checking that they need 27 minutes.

hints: First work out how many of the questions can possibly fit.
This is time triage: you are choosing a set of questions, not an order. Bound how many can fit, then test the biggest point totals from the top down until one fits in 15 minutes.
The four quickest questions need 3 + 4 + 5 + 7 = 19 minutes, so at most three fit. 14 points would need both 5-pointers and a 4-pointer. Check how long that takes, then check 13.

solutions.reliable: The four quickest questions take 3 + 4 + 5 + 7 = 19 minutes, so she can finish at most three. The best three-question total would be 5 + 5 + 4 = 14, but that needs at least 7 + 8 + 3 = 18 minutes. Next is 13 = 5 + 4 + 4, and the 7-minute 5-pointer with both 4-pointers takes 7 + 3 + 5 = 15 minutes exactly. So 13 is the most. The transferable idea: when time is short, pick the best set that fits, and do not trust a rule like most points first or quickest first.
solutions.elegant: Bound first, then search from the top: three questions at most, 14 is too slow, 13 fits exactly. Only two totals ever need checking.

whyOnTest: Late in a paper the choice is which questions, not which first, and greedy rules like most points first or quickest first leave points behind.
author: Devansh Sanghavi
